armadillo-removal.intro: Hodges is a small Greenwood County town in the rolling piedmont — a quiet community of older homes and farm properties in country that armadillos have colonised thoroughly in the last generation. Nine-banded armadillos root Hodges' lawns for grubs and worms, dig their burrows under porches, barn edges, and AC pads, and work the creek bottoms and field edges that surround the town. They are night animals and solitary ones, but a Hodges yard shows their work by morning: rooted beds, shallow feeding holes across the sod, and the burrow at the foundation that deepens a little every week until the slab edge or the porch footing is part of the excavation.
armadillo-removal.extendedBody:
Rooting, burrows, and the closing

Hodges armadillo work pairs trapping with burrow management, because the digging is two problems: the feeding rooting across the lawns, and the burrow system at the structures. We trap the animals working your ground — armadillos are creatures of routine, travelling the same fence lines and creek edges nightly, which is what makes them trappable by placement rather than bait — and then the burrows are backfilled and screened, because an open burrow in Hodges gets its next tenant within the season, armadillo or skunk or opossum. The grub conversation is part of the visit: a lawn carrying a heavy grub load is a feeding station, and treating it alongside the trapping ends the rooting rather than relocating it to the beds. Removal runs under the state's depredation-permit framework for your property. What armadillos are not is a house problem — they do not climb and they do not want your attic; they want your soil, and the work is scoped to the ground from the start.

faqs.q: How much does armadillo removal cost in Hodges?
faqs.a: It depends on the burrows — one animal rooting a lawn is a compact job; a burrow system at the foundation plus lawn damage across a farm property is a programme with backfill and screening in the quote. We walk the ground first, show you the active burrows and the feeding sign, and give one firm price for the trapping and closing together. The grub assessment is part of the walk, because in Hodges the food source decides whether the yard gets re-let.

faqs.q: An armadillo burrow is undermining our Hodges porch. How quickly does that get serious?
faqs.a: Faster than most animal damage — an armadillo burrow is a real excavation, several feet of tunnel with a chamber, and at a porch footing or slab edge it removes the soil the structure is standing on. We trap the resident, then backfill the system properly rather than capping the entrance, because a capped burrow with voids inside still settles. If the porch has already begun to dip, we will tell you plainly and document the extent, so you can decide about the structural side with the evidence in hand.

opossum-removal.intro: Opossum work in Hodges is under-structure work. Virginia opossums den under the older homes' porches, in the crawlspace edges, under the barns and well houses of this small Greenwood County farm community — solitary, nocturnal, and committed to any dry void within a nightly walk of food. Hodges' farm country feeds them well: pet food on porches, fallen fruit, the creeks' edges, and every unsealed bin in the community. The calls come when the den is too close — an opossum hissing from under the steps, a dog with a nightly appointment at the crawlspace vent, a mother raising a litter of young under the house through the spring. They are placid animals and easy tenants to evict, but the void they chose stays attractive after they leave.
opossum-removal.extendedBody:
Eviction is easy; the void is the job

A Hodges opossum removal is mostly carpentry. The animal itself is trapped or excluded without drama — opossums are not aggressive, they are actors, and the famous playing-dead routine is the whole of their defence. The durable part is closing the address: porch perimeters and crawlspace edges screened with mesh buried at the base, the under-barn gaps that matter blocked, so the next prospecting opossum — and in farm country there is always a next one by fall — finds the property closed. We time spring work honestly: a female denning with young in March is trapped as the family becomes mobile or excluded with the young accounted for, because an exclusion that seals a mother out and her litter in is a worse call in two weeks. Removal runs under the depredation permit for your property. And the food conversation is part of every Hodges visit — pet food in at night, bins sealed — because an opossum's territory is drawn around its dinner, and the map is redrawn the week the dinners move indoors.

faqs.q: How much does opossum removal cost in Hodges?
faqs.a: It depends on the den and the screening — one animal under a small porch is a compact job; a farmstead with voids under the house and the barn is a programme. We inspect first and quote the removal and the closing as one firm price, because eviction without screening in Hodges is a season's rental of the same void to the next tenant. If a mother with young is in residence, we will tell you the timing the family needs and price the job around it honestly.

faqs.q: An opossum under our Hodges porch plays dead when the dog finds it. Is it dangerous?
faqs.a: It is frightened, which is the opposite end of its abilities from dangerous. Opossums are among the least aggressive animals we handle — the hiss, the teeth, and the collapse are a performance, and it usually works. The genuine risks are small and manageable: keep the dog from cornering it nightly, which stresses both animals, and let us close the den so the performances end. One more thing in the opossum's favour, since Hodges is tick country: they are fastidious groomers that eat large numbers of ticks, so a passing opossum in the yard is a service; it is only the den under the house that needs to go.
